query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Coating hot-dip aluminum plating equipment with a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) that incorporates controlled, coherent nanoprecipitations will reduce erosion by high‐temperature liquid aluminum compared to conventional materials.
generation.material_initial_state: A bulk tungsten-based refractory HEA prepared with a microstructure engineered to include stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations.
generation.intervention: Apply the tungsten-based refractory HEA as a protective coating on parts (rollers, guide plates) used in the hot-dip aluminum plating process.
generation.conditions: Long-term exposure to high-temperature liquid aluminum during the dipping process under cyclic thermal loads.
generation.structural_mediator: The presence of coherent nanoprecipitates (SCCPs) within the HEA microstructure that promote a stable, protective oxide scale and enhance mechanical integrity.
generation.mechanism: The HEA is expected to form a robust protective oxide layer at the operating temperature that inhibits liquid aluminum penetration and corrosion. Simultaneously, the nanoprecipitates mitigate dislocation-driven degradation and improve high-temperature strength, effectively reducing erosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated parts will display significantly lower erosion rates and improved structural stability during prolonged exposure to liquid aluminum compared to uncoated or conventionally coated equipment.
generation.baseline: Traditional dipping/plating equipment materials that experience accelerated corrosion and material loss when in direct contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum.
generation.boundary: This protective effect is predicted under steady high-temperature conditions typical of the hot-dip process; performance under rapid thermal cycling or in the presence of additional chemical aggressors remains to be established.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties include the long-term adhesion and thermal cycling performance of the HEA coating and its precise interaction with molten aluminum, which require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of identical dipping/plating equipment parts: one group coated with the tungsten-based refractory HEA and one group with conventional materials. Expose both groups to repeated hot-dip cycles in liquid aluminum at operating temperatures over an extended period.
measurements: Quantitative erosion rate (mass loss per unit area)
Microstructural analysis of the coating and oxide scale via SEM/TEM
Mechanical integrity tests (e.g., tensile or creep tests) after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-based HEA coated parts do not show a statistically significant reduction in erosion rate and maintenance of microstructural integrity compared to the conventional parts, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date.
